decks.title: Ecosystem — Part 1: Structure, productivity and decomposition
goals: Define an ecosystem, name its types, and describe the structure and function of a pond
Distinguish GPP, NPP and secondary productivity; explain PAR, standing crop and standing state
Describe the steps of decomposition and the factors that affect its rate

slides.heading: The ecosystem
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what an ecosystem is, how much it produces, and how dead matter is recycled.

visual.alt: Cycle from abiotic components to producers, consumers and decomposers and back

slides.narration: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with their physical surroundings. Energy flows through it, and nutrients are cycled back again and again.

slides.heading: Types and components of ecosystems
slides.body_md: Ecosystems vary in size from a small pond to a large forest or sea.

visual.alt: Table of types and components of ecosystems

slides.narration: Whatever its size, every ecosystem has living parts and non-living parts that interact. The forest, grassland and desert are terrestrial; ponds, lakes, rivers and estuaries are aquatic; crop fields and aquaria are made by people.

slides.heading: A pond ecosystem
slides.body_md: A pond is a shallow water body showing all the basic components of an ecosystem.

slides.narration: Phytoplankton, algae and floating, submerged and marginal plants are the producers. Zooplankton and free-swimming and bottom-dwelling animals are consumers. Fungi, bacteria and flagellates at the bottom decompose dead matter, and sunlight, temperature and dissolved substances are the abiotic components.

slides.heading: How a pond works
slides.body_md: A pond performs all the functions of an ecosystem.

rows: Autotrophs convert inorganic materials into organic matter using sunlight
Dead organic matter is broken down and minerals are released for reuse
Energy moves one way to higher trophic levels and is lost as heat

visual.alt: Table of functions of a pond ecosystem

slides.narration: In a pond, as in any ecosystem, materials go round in cycles but energy passes through only once. Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked in dead bodies.

slides.heading: Quick check: pond
slides.body_md: Which are the producers in a pond?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which organisms make food by photosynthesis?

slides.heading: Productivity
slides.body_md: **Primary production** is the amount of biomass produced per unit area over a time period by plants; its rate is **productivity**, in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. **Gross primary productivity (GPP)** is the rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis; some is used in **respiration (R)**. **Net primary productivity: NPP = GPP − R**, available to heterotrophs. **Secondary productivity** is the rate of formation of new organic matter by **consumers**.

rows: Organic matter used by plants in respiration
GPP − R; available to consumers and decomposers
Rate of new biomass made by consumers

visual.alt: Table of productivity terms

slides.narration: Plants use part of what they make to stay alive. What is left over, the net primary productivity, is the food available to every other organism in the ecosystem.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: net primary productivity
slides.body_md: A grassland has a GPP of 25000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹, and its plants use 9000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ in respiration. Find the NPP and the percentage of GPP available to consumers.
bullets: $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = 25000 - 9000 = 16000$ kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Percentage $= \dfrac{16000}{25000} \times 100 = 64$ percent.

visual.alt: Worked table: NPP 16000, 64 percent of GPP

slides.narration: Subtract what the plants respire from what they produce. Here a little under two thirds of the gross production is left for herbivores and decomposers.

slides.heading: PAR, global productivity, standing crop and standing state
slides.body_md: Only part of sunlight can drive photosynthesis.

rows: About 50 percent of incident solar radiation; plants capture only 2–10 percent of PAR
About 170 billion tons (dry weight) a year; oceans give only about 55 billion tons though they cover about 70 percent of the surface
Amount of living material (biomass) at each trophic level at a particular time
Amount of nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and calcium in the soil at a given time

visual.alt: Table of PAR, global productivity, standing crop and standing state

slides.narration: Although oceans cover most of the Earth, they are less productive than land, mainly because nutrients are scarce in open water. Standing crop is living biomass; standing state is the store of nutrients in the soil.

slides.heading: Decomposition
slides.body_md: **Decomposers** break down complex organic matter (**detritus**: dead leaves, bark, flowers, animal remains, faeces) into inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water and nutrients.

rows: Detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into small particles
Water-soluble inorganic nutrients move down into the soil and are precipitated as unavailable salts
Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances
Dark, amorphous humus accumulates; it resists microbes and decomposes very slowly; it stores nutrients
Some microbes degrade humus further, releasing inorganic nutrients

visual.alt: Table of the steps of decomposition

slides.narration: All these steps go on at the same time on the same pieces of detritus. Humus is a colloid that holds nutrients for a long time, and mineralisation slowly releases them for plants to use again.

slides.heading: Climate and the rate of decomposition
slides.body_md: **Warm and moist** conditions favour decomposition; **low temperature** and **anaerobic** conditions slow it, so organic matter builds up.

slides.narration: The curves show the same litter decomposing in two habitats. In a warm, wet forest, most leaves have disappeared within a year. In a cold or waterlogged place, they last much longer, which is why peat and thick litter accumulate there.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: comparing decomposition
slides.body_md: Using the model M = M₀e^{−kt} with k = 0.25 per month (warm, moist forest) and k = 0.03 per month (cold, dry habitat), what percentage of 100 g of litter remains after 6 months in each?
bullets: Warm: $100 \times e^{-0.25 \times 6} = 22.3$ g.
Cold: $100 \times e^{-0.03 \times 6} = 83.5$ g.
Warmth and moisture speed up microbial activity, so litter vanishes far faster in the forest.

visual.alt: Worked table: 22.3 grams versus 83.5 grams

slides.narration: In the warm forest less than a quarter of the litter remains after six months, while in the cold, dry habitat more than four fifths is still there. Temperature and moisture strongly control decomposers.

slides.heading: Factors affecting decomposition
slides.body_md: The rate depends on the detritus itself and on the climate.

rows: Nitrogen and water-soluble sugars in detritus
Inhibit decomposers: slow; organic matter builds up

visual.alt: Table of factors affecting decomposition

slides.narration: Woody material rich in lignin, and insect shells rich in chitin, rot slowly. Soft, nitrogen-rich leaves rot quickly. Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process, so waterlogged soils store organic matter.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ecosystem: functional unit; terrestrial, aquatic, man-made; biotic and abiotic components.
Pond: producers (phytoplankton, plants), consumers (zooplankton, fish), decomposers (bacteria, fungi), abiotic components.
Productivity: GPP, NPP = GPP − R, secondary productivity; PAR (2–10 percent captured); standing crop and standing state.
Decomposition: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation.
Rate: slow with lignin, chitin, cold, anaerobic conditions; fast with nitrogen, sugars, warmth, moisture.

visual.alt: Summary table of key terms

slides.narration: To recap: an ecosystem has living and non-living parts, plants produce organic matter at a measurable rate, and decomposers return nutrients through a series of steps whose speed depends on the litter and the climate.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Use **NPP = GPP − R** with units.
Give the **five steps** of decomposition in order.
Distinguish **standing crop** from **standing state**.
Describe the **pond** with producers, consumers, decomposers and abiotic components.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the productivity equation with units. Learn the steps of decomposition in order. Keep standing crop and standing state apart. And describe a pond with all its components.

goals: Distinguish grazing and detritus food chains, and explain food webs and trophic levels
Apply the 10 percent law to energy flow
Describe pyramids of number, biomass and energy, with upright and inverted examples

slides.heading: Energy in ecosystems
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how energy moves through food chains and webs, and how it shapes ecological pyramids.

visual.alt: Flow of energy from the sun through producers, herbivores and carnivores, ending as heat

slides.narration: Except for deep-sea communities around hydrothermal vents, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems. Energy passes in one direction, from producers to consumers, and is lost as heat at every step.

slides.heading: Food chains
slides.body_md: There are two main kinds of food chain.

rows: Terrestrial ecosystems (a larger fraction of energy)

visual.alt: Table comparing grazing and detritus food chains

slides.narration: In a forest, most leaves are never eaten by herbivores; they fall and are broken down. So in land ecosystems more energy flows through the detritus food chain. The two chains are linked, because detritivores may be eaten by grazing-chain animals.

slides.heading: Food webs and trophic levels
slides.body_md: Natural food chains are interconnected into a **food web**. Each organism occupies a **trophic level** according to its source of food.

visual.alt: Table of trophic levels and members

slides.narration: A food web is more realistic than a single chain, because most animals eat more than one kind of food. A species may even feed at more than one trophic level at the same time.

slides.heading: Energy flow and the 10 percent law
slides.body_md: At each transfer, most energy is used in respiration and lost as **heat**; only about **10 percent** passes to the next trophic level (**Lindeman’s 10 percent law**). Energy flow is therefore **unidirectional**, and the number of trophic levels is **limited**.

slides.narration: Because only a tenth of the energy reaches each higher level, there is too little energy left after four or five transfers to support another level. That is why food chains are short.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: applying the 10 percent law
slides.body_md: Producers in a lake trap 50000 J of energy. Using the 10 percent law, how much energy reaches primary, secondary and tertiary consumers? What is the transfer efficiency?
bullets: Primary $= 50000 \times 0.1 = 5000$ J; secondary $= 500$ J; tertiary $= 50$ J.
Efficiency $= \dfrac{5000}{50000} \times 100 = 10$ percent at each step.

visual.alt: Worked table: 50 J reaches tertiary consumers

slides.narration: Multiply by one tenth at each step. Only one thousandth of the producers’ energy reaches the top carnivores, which is why there are so few of them.

slides.body_md: The relation between trophic levels can be shown as pyramids of **number**, **biomass** or **energy**, with **producers at the base** and top carnivores at the apex.

sections.heading: 1. Ecosystem: structure and the pond
sections.body_md:
An **ecosystem** is a **functional unit of nature** where living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding physical environment. Ecosystems vary greatly in size — from a small pond to a large forest or sea; the whole **biosphere** may be regarded as a global ecosystem.

**Types:** **terrestrial** (forest, grassland, desert) and **aquatic** (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary); **man-made** ecosystems include crop fields and aquaria.

**Components:** **biotic** — producers (autotrophs), consumers (heterotrophs) and decomposers; **abiotic** — water, soil, minerals, light, temperature and other physical factors. Interaction of biotic and abiotic components gives a physical **structure** to an ecosystem, characterised by **species composition** and **stratification** (vertical distribution of species at different levels, for example trees, shrubs and herbs in a forest).

**The pond ecosystem:** a shallow water body in which all the basic components can be studied.
- **Abiotic:** water with **dissolved inorganic and organic substances** and the rich **soil deposit** at the bottom; the **solar input**, cycle of temperature, day length and other climatic conditions regulate the rate of function of the whole pond.
- **Producers (autotrophs):** **phytoplankton**, some algae, and **floating, submerged and marginal plants** along the edges.
- **Consumers:** **zooplankton** and **free-swimming and bottom-dwelling** forms.
- **Decomposers:** **fungi, bacteria and flagellates**, especially abundant at the **bottom**.

**Functions:** (i) **conversion of inorganic into organic material** with radiant energy by autotrophs; (ii) **consumption** of autotrophs by heterotrophs; (iii) **decomposition and mineralisation** of dead organic matter, releasing minerals for reuse; (iv) **unidirectional movement of energy** towards higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as **heat**.

key_terms.definition_md: Functional unit of nature with interacting organisms and physical environment.
Vertical distribution of species at different levels.
Microscopic floating photosynthetic organisms; producers in water.

sections.heading: 2. Productivity
sections.body_md:
A constant input of **solar energy** is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain itself.
- **Primary production** is the amount of **biomass or organic matter** produced per unit area over a time period by plants during **photosynthesis**, expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²). The **rate** of biomass production is **productivity** (g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹).
- **Gross primary productivity (GPP)** is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable amount is used by plants in **respiration (R)**.
- **Net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP − R**: the biomass available for consumption by **heterotrophs** (herbivores and decomposers). Example: GPP 25000 − R 9000 = NPP 16000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.
- **Secondary productivity** is the rate of formation of **new organic matter by consumers**.
Primary productivity depends on the plant species, environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity, so it varies between ecosystems. The **annual NPP of the whole biosphere** is about **170 billion tons** (dry weight) of organic matter; **oceans**, despite covering about **70 percent** of the surface, produce only about **55 billion tons**.

**Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)** is about **50 percent** of the incident solar radiation; plants capture only **2–10 percent of PAR**, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.

**Standing crop** — the mass of living material (**biomass**) at each trophic level at a particular time (as fresh or dry weight per unit area). **Standing state** — the amount of **nutrients** such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and calcium present in the **soil** at any given time.

key_terms.definition_md: Rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis.
GPP minus respiration; available to heterotrophs.
Photosynthetically active radiation, about half of incident sunlight.

sections.heading: 3. Decomposition
sections.body_md:
**Decomposers** break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances such as **carbon dioxide, water and nutrients**; this process is **decomposition**. Dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead remains of animals, including faecal matter, form **detritus**, the raw material.

**Steps** (operating simultaneously on the detritus):
1. **Fragmentation** — **detritivores** such as **earthworms** break down detritus into **smaller particles**.
2. **Leaching** — **water-soluble inorganic nutrients** go down into the soil horizon and get **precipitated as unavailable salts**.
3. **Catabolism** — **bacterial and fungal enzymes** degrade detritus into **simpler inorganic substances**.
4. **Humification** — accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous substance called **humus**, which is **highly resistant** to microbial action and decomposes **extremely slowly**; being **colloidal**, it serves as a **reservoir of nutrients**.
5. **Mineralisation** — humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing **inorganic nutrients**.

**Factors affecting the rate:** decomposition is largely an **oxygen-requiring** process. The rate is controlled by the **chemical composition** of the detritus — **slower** if it is rich in **lignin and chitin**, **quicker** if rich in **nitrogen and water-soluble substances such as sugars** — and by **climatic factors**: **warm and moist** environments favour it, whereas **low temperature and anaerobiosis** inhibit it, resulting in a build-up of organic material.

key_terms.definition_md: Dead plant and animal remains, the raw material of decomposition.
Formation of humus, which resists decomposition.
Release of inorganic nutrients from humus.
Washing of soluble nutrients down into the soil.

sections.heading: 4. Energy flow
sections.body_md:
Except for deep-sea **hydrothermal** ecosystems, the **sun** is the only source of energy for all ecosystems. Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 percent is PAR, and plants capture only 2–10 percent of it. Energy flow is **unidirectional**: from the sun to **producers** and then to **consumers**; it obeys the laws of thermodynamics, and at every transfer a great deal is lost as **heat**.

**Food chains:**
- **Grazing food chain (GFC)** — starts with living producers: grass → goat → man. In **aquatic** ecosystems the GFC is the **major conduit** for energy flow.
- **Detritus food chain (DFC)** — begins with **dead organic matter**; made up of **decomposers** (heterotrophic **saprotrophs**: fungi and bacteria) and detritivores. In **terrestrial** ecosystems a much **larger fraction** of energy flows through the DFC than through the GFC. The DFC may be connected with the GFC, as some DFC organisms are prey to GFC animals.
- **Food web** — natural interconnection of food chains.

**Trophic levels:** organisms occupy a place in the food chain according to their feeding relationship: **producers** (first), **herbivores or primary consumers** (second), **primary carnivores or secondary consumers** (third), **secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers** (fourth). A species may occupy more than one trophic level in the same ecosystem at the same time.

**10 percent law (Lindeman):** only about **10 percent** of the energy is transferred to each higher trophic level from the lower one (for example 20000 → 2000 → 200 → 20 J). Hence the number of trophic levels is limited.

sections.heading: 5. Ecological pyramids
sections.body_md:
The relationship between organisms at different trophic levels, in terms of **number, biomass or energy**, can be shown as a **pyramid**. The **base** represents the **producers** (first trophic level) and the **apex** the top-level consumers.
- **Pyramid of numbers** — usually **upright** (grassland: many grasses, fewer herbivores, few carnivores). It can be **inverted**: for example, **a single tree** supports a large number of **insects**, which support fewer birds.
- **Pyramid of biomass** — usually upright on land. In the **sea** it is generally **inverted**, because the **biomass of fishes** (and zooplankton) far exceeds that of the fast-reproducing **phytoplankton** at any one time.
- **Pyramid of energy** — **always upright** and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some is always **lost as heat** at each step.

**Limitations:** pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to **two or more trophic levels**; they assume a **simple food chain**, which almost never exists in nature, and do not accommodate a **food web**; and **saprophytes** are not given any place, although they play a vital role.

key_terms.definition_md: Always upright, as energy is lost at every level.
In the sea, consumer biomass exceeds phytoplankton biomass.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing NPP = GPP + R (it is GPP − R).
- Confusing standing crop (biomass) with standing state (nutrients in soil).
- Saying humus decomposes quickly (it is highly resistant).
- Saying the grazing food chain carries most energy on land (the detritus food chain does).
- Saying the pyramid of energy can be inverted (never).
- Giving the 10 percent law as 10 percent lost (about 90 percent is lost; 10 percent passes on).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a producer, a step of decomposition, a value of PAR, a pyramid that can be inverted.
- 2–3-mark questions: GPP vs NPP; standing crop vs state; steps of decomposition; GFC vs DFC; 10 percent law.
- 5-mark questions in parts: pond ecosystem; decomposition with factors; energy flow with pyramids.

questions.stem_md: The vertical distribution of species at different levels in an ecosystem, such as trees, shrubs and herbs in a forest, is called ______.
Define an ecosystem and name its biotic and abiotic components.

answer.model_answer_md: An **ecosystem** is a **functional unit of nature** in which living organisms **interact** among themselves and with their **physical environment**. **Biotic** components are **producers, consumers and decomposers**; **abiotic** components include **water, soil, minerals, light and temperature**.

questions.stem_md: State the four functions performed by a pond ecosystem.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Conversion of inorganic into organic material** by autotrophs using sunlight; (ii) **consumption** of autotrophs by **heterotrophs**; (iii) **decomposition and mineralisation** of dead organic matter, releasing minerals for reuse; (iv) **unidirectional flow of energy** to higher trophic levels, with **loss as heat**.

questions.stem_md: A class studies the pond in its school garden. Describe the producers, consumers, decomposers and abiotic components they should record.

answer.model_answer_md: **Producers:** **phytoplankton**, algae, and **floating, submerged and marginal plants**. **Consumers:** **zooplankton** and **free-swimming and bottom-dwelling** animals such as fish, insects and snails. **Decomposers:** **bacteria, fungi and flagellates**, mostly in the **bottom mud**. **Abiotic components:** **water** with **dissolved inorganic and organic substances**, the **soil deposit** at the bottom, and **sunlight, temperature and day length**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a pond ecosystem showing its components. [2]
(b) Explain the functions of a pond ecosystem. [2]
(c) If all decomposers in a pond were killed, what would happen over time? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a pond with **sunlight**; **phytoplankton**, **floating**, **submerged** and **marginal plants** (producers); **zooplankton** and **fish** (consumers); **bacteria and fungi** in the **bottom mud** (decomposers); **water with dissolved substances** and **soil deposit** (abiotic).

(b) **Producers** convert inorganic materials into organic matter using sunlight; **consumers** eat them; **decomposers** break down dead matter and **mineralise** it; **energy** flows one way and is lost as **heat**.

(c) Dead matter would **accumulate**; **nutrients** would stay locked in it and not be **recycled**, so the producers would run short of minerals and the whole ecosystem would **decline**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Net primary productivity is always less than gross primary productivity.

**Reason (R):** Plants use part of the organic matter they produce in respiration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and respiratory loss (NPP = GPP − R) explains the difference — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is the

options.text_md: amount of nutrients in the soil at a given time
rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers
biomass at each trophic level at a particular time
rate of production of organic matter by plants during photosynthesis

questions.solution_md: GPP is total photosynthetic production per unit area per unit time — option (d).

questions.stem_md: About what fraction of the incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
questions.solution_md: PAR is about half of incident radiation; plants capture 2–10 percent of PAR — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Oceans cover about 70 percent of the Earth’s surface but contribute only about a third of global net primary productivity. What is the main reason?

options.text_md: Open ocean water is poor in nutrients, which limits phytoplankton growth.
Sunlight does not reach the ocean surface.

questions.solution_md: Nutrient scarcity limits primary productivity in most of the ocean — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The amount of nitrogen, phosphorus and calcium present in the soil of an ecosystem at a given time is its
questions.solution_md: Standing state refers to nutrients; standing crop to living biomass — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The rate at which herbivores and carnivores in a grassland form new organic matter is called
questions.solution_md: Secondary productivity is production by consumers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Of the global annual net primary productivity of about 170 billion tons, the oceans contribute only about ______ billion tons.
A wheat field has a gross primary productivity of 18 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹, and the wheat plants respire 7500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. What is the net primary productivity?
In a lake, phytoplankton have a GPP of 12 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and lose 4200 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ in respiration. What percentage of GPP is available to consumers as NPP?
A forest has a GPP of 20 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and an NPP of 12 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. How much energy do its plants use in respiration?
A field receives 100 000 J of solar radiation. If PAR is 50 percent of this and the crop captures 4 percent of the PAR, how many joules are captured in photosynthesis?
Distinguish between standing crop and standing state of an ecosystem.

answer.model_answer_md: **Standing crop** is the **mass of living material (biomass)** present at each **trophic level** at a particular time, measured as fresh or dry weight per unit area. **Standing state** is the amount of **nutrients** — carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium — present in the **soil** at any given time.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between gross primary productivity, net primary productivity and secondary productivity, and write the relation between the first two.

answer.model_answer_md: **GPP** is the **rate of production of organic matter** by plants during **photosynthesis**. Part of it is used by the plants in **respiration (R)**. **NPP** is what remains, **NPP = GPP − R**, and is available to **herbivores and decomposers**. **Secondary productivity** is the **rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers**. All are expressed per unit area per unit time (g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹).

questions.stem_md: Of 2 000 000 J of sunlight falling on a pasture, half is PAR and the grass captures 2 percent of the PAR. Calculate the energy captured and comment on why this small fraction matters for the whole ecosystem.

answer.model_answer_md: PAR = 2 000 000 × 0.5 = **1 000 000 J**; captured = 1 000 000 × 0.02 = **20000 J**. Plants capture only **2–10 percent of PAR**, yet this small amount is the **only energy input** for herbivores, carnivores and decomposers; everything else in the ecosystem depends on it, and much of it is later **lost as heat**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define primary productivity and state its units. [1]
(b) Explain GPP, NPP and the relation between them. [2]
(c) A tropical rain forest has GPP 30 000 and R 18 000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; a grassland has GPP 12 000 and R 4000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. Which has the higher NPP, and which converts the higher percentage of GPP into NPP? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Primary productivity** is the **rate of biomass production** by plants per unit area, in **g m⁻² yr⁻¹** or **kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹**.

(b) **GPP** is the rate of production of organic matter in **photosynthesis**; part is used in **respiration (R)**; **NPP = GPP − R** is available to **heterotrophs**.

(c) Forest NPP = **12000**; grassland NPP = **8000**. The **forest** has the higher NPP, but the **grassland** converts a higher percentage of GPP (**66.7 percent** vs **40 percent**), as forest trees respire much more.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is detritus? Name two detritivores or decomposers. [1]
(b) Describe the five steps of decomposition. [3]
(c) Explain why leaf litter in a tropical rain forest disappears much faster than in a coniferous forest of a cold region. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Detritus** is dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal remains including **faecal matter**; e.g. **earthworms** (detritivores), **bacteria and fungi** (decomposers).

(b) **Fragmentation** by detritivores into small particles; **leaching** of soluble nutrients into the soil, precipitated as salts; **catabolism** by bacterial and fungal **enzymes** into simpler inorganic substances; **humification** to resistant, dark **humus**; **mineralisation** of humus releasing inorganic nutrients.

(c) The rain forest is **warm and moist**, favouring rapid microbial activity; the cold forest has **low temperatures** and needle litter rich in **resistant compounds**, so decomposition is **slow**.

questions.stem_md: The 10 percent law of energy transfer between trophic levels was proposed by ______.

What is a food web? Why is it a more realistic picture of an ecosystem than a food chain?

answer.model_answer_md: A **food web** is a network of **interconnected food chains** in an ecosystem. It is more realistic because most animals eat **more than one kind of food** and are eaten by **more than one predator**, and a species may feed at **more than one trophic level**; a single chain ignores these links.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the grazing food chain and the detritus food chain, giving an example of each, and state in which kind of ecosystem each carries more energy.

answer.model_answer_md: The **grazing food chain** begins with **living green plants** (producers) and passes to herbivores and carnivores — for example **grass → goat → man**; it is the **major conduit** in **aquatic** ecosystems. The **detritus food chain** begins with **dead organic matter** and involves **decomposers** (saprotrophic fungi and bacteria) and detritivores — for example **dead leaves → earthworm → bird**; in **terrestrial** ecosystems a much **larger fraction** of energy flows through it.

questions.stem_md: Explain why food chains in nature rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy flow is **unidirectional**, and at each transfer only about **10 percent** of the energy passes to the next level (**10 percent law**); the rest is used in **respiration** and lost as **heat**, or remains unused. After four or five transfers, only a **tiny fraction** of the energy fixed by producers remains — too little to support a **viable population** of a further level of consumers.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why energy flow in an ecosystem is described as unidirectional. [1]
(b) State the 10 percent law. If producers fix 60 000 J, how much energy reaches each of the next three trophic levels? [2]
(c) Draw a pyramid of energy for this chain and explain why it can never be inverted. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Energy passes from the **sun to producers to consumers** and is lost as **heat** at each level; it **does not return** to the sun or to producers.

(b) Only about **10 percent** of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next (**Lindeman**). Primary consumers **6000 J**, secondary **600 J**, tertiary **60 J**.

(c) **Diagram:** four stacked bars narrowing upwards — producers **60000**, then **6000**, **600**, **60 J**. Energy is **lost as heat** at every transfer, so each level must have **less** energy than the one below; the pyramid is **always upright**.

questions.stem_md: State two limitations of ecological pyramids.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) They assume a **simple food chain**, which almost never exists in nature, and cannot show a **food web**. questions.stem_md: Describe the pyramids of number, biomass and energy, giving one example of an upright and one of an inverted pyramid where possible.

answer.model_answer_md: **Pyramid of numbers:** upright in a **grassland** (many grasses, fewer herbivores, few carnivores); **inverted** for a **single tree** supporting many insects. **Pyramid of biomass:** upright on land; **inverted in the sea**, where fish and zooplankton biomass exceeds that of phytoplankton. **Pyramid of energy:** **always upright**, because energy is **lost as heat** at each level; it can **never** be inverted.
